title: D2 — physical storage contract (Delta in OneLake)
description: Machine-readable contract for how FOCUS cost data is physically materialized in OneLake. Defines the managed Delta table, physical types, partitioning, Z-order, and the compaction service-level expectation. The compaction-with-metrics notebook and the DirectLake-readiness gate both load this file and FAIL LOUDLY when reality drifts from it. Do NOT assert these targets in documentation only — this file is the spec.

storageMode.rationale: Decision 2: managed Delta tables, not shortcuts. Shortcuts inherit the source small-file problem and cannot be compacted or Z-ordered, so they cannot remove the $2-5M/month query ceiling. Managed Delta with daily compaction is the only option that does.

rejected.shortcut: Inherits small-file fragmentation; not compactable or Z-orderable. Same problem, different door.

table.name: Costs
table.note: Column set and FOCUS version are owned by the D1 logical contract. This file owns only the PHYSICAL representation.

physicalTypeMapping.description: Maps each D1 logical type to the physical Delta/Spark type written to OneLake. Cost/price measures use double (FOCUS 'real'), matching the toolkit v1_2 decision to use real over decimal for performance at scale.

decimal.rationale: Toolkit Hub schema v1_2 converts cost/price measures from decimal to real (double) for query performance. The Delta layout matches that physical choice.

json.rationale: FOCUS Tags (and other JSON columns) are stored as a JSON-encoded string rather than a complex map type, because DirectLake has limited support for nested/complex types. Keeping them as strings preserves the DirectLake-readiness path (Decision 4).

partitioning.description: Partition by charge period month. Aligns with the dominant time-range filter in cost reporting and keeps partition counts bounded.
partitioning.derivation: x_ChargeMonth = date_trunc('month', ChargePeriodStart), stored as a DATE for partition pruning.
partitioning.note: ChargePeriodStart itself is high-cardinality (daily); a derived month column keeps partitions coarse.

zorder.rationale: Reasonable default: these are the most common high-cardinality filter/group dimensions in multi-account, multi-subscription cost analysis.
zorder.validationRequired: Confirm against the pilot customer's ACTUAL dominant query filters before locking in (Phase 6). Treat as provisional until one full billing cycle of query telemetry exists. Re-running OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY with different columns is non-destructive, so this is safe to revise.
zorder.subscriptionIdNote: FOCUS 1.2 names the subscription-level scope SubAccountId. Updated from the provisional SubscriptionId placeholder.

compaction.description: Compaction is treated as a MONITORED SLA, not a fire-and-forget scheduled job. It is load-bearing for query performance AND for the DirectLake-readiness gate, and is the easiest thing to silently stop running.

sla.note: 26h tolerance allows one missed daily window before alerting. Breaching any threshold must raise an alert (Data Activator / monitoring), not silently degrade queries. These are PRODUCTION thresholds; a small pilot/test dataset that cannot reach the 64MB floor should pass pilot-scale sla_overrides to validate_compaction_sla at the call site (see 03_compaction) rather than lowering these values.

metrics.description: Emitted on every run to a location an alert can watch. These are the inputs to both the SLA check and the DirectLake-readiness gate.

sink.name: _pilot_compaction_metrics
sink.note: Append-only operational table; one row per run. Watchable by Data Activator or a scheduled alert query.

directLake.description: Guardrails consumed by the DirectLake-readiness gate (Decision 4). DirectLake silently falls back to DirectQuery above these limits, so they are checked, not assumed. Defaults are conservative and SKU-agnostic; raise them only when validated against the pilot capacity SKU's published DirectLake limits.
directLake.note: minAvgFileSizeMB mirrors the compaction SLA floor so a table that passes compaction is sized appropriately for DirectLake memory-mapping.

rowConservation.description: Every materialization hop (source->staging in ingestion, staging->Delta in the write) must neither drop nor invent rows. Real hub failures change the row count with NO error: extents silently lost during multi-file ingestion, or rows dropped when a manifest row count is null. The notebooks capture the input and output counts of each hop and hand them to validate_row_conservation, which fails loudly on any drift beyond the tolerance below so a silent loss stops the pipeline instead of corrupting cost totals downstream.
rowConservation.note: 0.0 means exact conservation (input count must equal output count). This is a physical copy/append, not a transform, so no rows should be added or removed; KQL remains the single transform owner (Decision 1). Raise this only if a hop legitimately dedupes or filters, and document why.

batchHandoff.description: Ingestion (notebook 01) and the Delta write (notebook 02) run as separate executions connected only by staging files in OneLake, whose listing can lag (see README OneLake sync notes). A partial staging read in notebook 02 would still pass that notebook's own row-conservation check because it conserves whatever subset it read — the loss is silent. This is the cross-boundary form of the #1625 / #2173 'processed a subset, assumed the whole' trap. To close it, notebook 01 writes an authoritative batch manifest (expected row count) and notebook 02 asserts, via validate_batch_completeness, that it consumed exactly that many rows before writing anything to Delta.
batchHandoff.note: Mirrors how the toolkit hub uses manifest.json row counts — the exact mechanism issue #2173 shows failing when the count is null. The manifest count is authoritative, so completeness is an exact-equality check with no tolerance.

enforcement.description: Policy applied by the compaction notebook and the readiness gate. Every rule maps to a silent-failure scenario from the decision deck.
